newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S.'s Albright in China, vows wide-ranging talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S.'s Albright in China, vows wide-ranging talks.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrived in Beijing on Monday for talks with the successors to the late Chinese patriarch Deng Xiaoping, vowing to engage them on issues from human rights to the environment.
Albright, on the last stop of a nine-nation tour, stepped off her plane only hours after the Chinese leader's body arrived at the Babaoshan cemetery, west of the capital, for cremation.
"I'm going to talk across the board on all the issues that we have been talking about," she told staff at the U.S. embassy in Beijing shortly after her arrival.
The issues would range from human rights to cooperation over North Korea and Cambodia as well as the environment, she said.
"My main mission is to engage with China and make them realise we want them to be part of our international community," she said.
U.S. officials tried to play down hopes of a breakthrough on thorny human rights issues, despite a New York Times report saying the two sides appeared within striking range of a deal.
"I don't believe the story in the New York Times is accurate," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.
"We've received no indication that a major breakthough of the kind described in the New York Times is imminent."

The New York Times said that under the possible deal China would agree to sign two key international covenants on human rights, release a represesentative group of at least eight prisoners and restart talks with the International Committee of the Red Cross for a programme of prison visits to determine the status of prisoners of conscience in China.
In return, Beijing could expect an end to the annual confrontation over its human rights record at the United Nations Commission on Human Rights in Geneva.

U.S. officials have said that Washington does not expect the death of Deng Xiaoping to bring any quick improvement in human rights in China and plans to proceed with a U.N. resolution faulting Beijing's record.
China is the last stop on Albright's nine-nation tour of European and Asian capitals, her first overseas trip since taking office last month.
She will meet President Jiang Zemin, Premier Li Peng and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen. She is due to leave early on Tuesday, before Deng's memorial rites at Beijing's Great Hall of the People.
Before boarding her flight from Tokyo to China on Monday morning, Albright had a breakfast meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

Officials said that, while the Beijing trip is important, they did not expect major progress on any of the issues to be discussed, including human rights, trade, Taiwan, Hong Kong and nuclear non-proliferation.

"The emphasis in China over the coming weeks and months is likely to be on continuity, on stability within the leadership, on building consensus within the leadership, in other words nothing risky," said a senior official, who briefed reporters on condition of anonymity.
"Our expectations should not be too high," he said.
"Based on the current situation we expect to proceed with the (U.N. human rights) resolution," the official said. Most European Union members shared the U.S. view of the situation, he said.

Albright, interviewed on ABC Television's "This Week", said Chinese leaders "expect me to raise human rights as an issue and I will". But she did not say what she would do on the resolution, which in the past has greatly angered Beijing.
